paper.title: Bias in odds ratios by logistic regression modelling and sample size
paper.citation: Nemes S, Jonasson JM, Genell A, Steineck G. BMC Medical Research Methodology 9:56 (2009)

seed.what: One population of 100,000 drawn once with seed 2724427 (the paper gives no seed); samples of size n drawn with a seed derived from it and n
seed.sensitivity: Over 20 other populations the Table 1 values move as shown in the seed-spread columns of tables.json

glm.what: Each sample fitted with R's glm.fit (binomial family, default control); the paper names no fitting function (Additional file 1 points to Harrell's Design library)
glm.sensitivity: glm.fit and Design's lrm reach the same maximum likelihood estimate when it exists; they differ only in which separated samples fail, see the separation rule

separation.what: Samples without a finite estimate left out: any fitted probability within 1e-8 of 0 or 1, or no convergence (the paper does not say how it handled them)
separation.sensitivity: Leaving out only the fits R warns about, or keeping every fit, changes the discrete slope and R squared most (tables.json, sensitivity columns)

ols_means.what: Table 1's OLS fits the 281 per-size means, the points Fig. 1 draws (the paper does not say means or individual estimates)
ols_means.sensitivity: The fit to all individual estimates gives nearly the same estimates and SEs but an R squared near 0.02, far from the paper's 0.963 and 0.836

axes.what: Our figures are drawn on the published axes, fitted to the published tick marks (largest residual 0.72 px)
axes.sensitivity: The tick fits leave under 1 px of error; the scores use a 2 px tolerance

kernel.what: lokern::lokerns (local plug-in bandwidth) for the kernel derivative, and a log-log slope within 2 ± 0.5 between n = 150 and 1400 as confirming a 1/n convergence (the paper names no software and reports no numbers)
kernel.sensitivity: The continuous slope is near -2; the result would change only if the band were narrower than its distance from -2

vline.what: Fig. 2's vertical line drawn at 2, the population value; the paper does not say (at n = 1000 the heading 2.003 and 2 are 0.4 px apart)
vline.sensitivity: The line is masked (2 px either side) before scoring

items.label: Table 1, continuous variable (intercept and n⁻¹: estimate, SE, t, p)

cause.summary: The intercept is the population draw: 2.011 lies inside our 20 populations (1.962 to 2.023; ours 1.966). The n⁻¹ slope and both SEs do not: b1 is 26.7 to 30.0 over 20 populations against 23.9, and the SEs are about 1.5 times the paper's, because our per-size means scatter more. The analytic first-order bias of our population is 23.8, close to the paper's 23.9. A population with x of SD 1 comes closer (b1 25.2, SE 0.307, intercept SE 0.00080) but does not close the gap.

items.label: Table 1, discrete variable (intercept and n⁻¹: estimate, SE, t, p)

cause.summary: The intercept is the population draw: -0.898 lies inside our 20 populations (-0.956 to -0.866; ours -0.855 is the far end of that spread). The slope does not come back: -1.9 here and -2.4 to -5.7 over 20 populations against -9.524, with SEs 2 to 3 times the paper's. Leaving out separated samples pulls the small-n means of the discrete coefficient toward zero; keeping the fits R does not warn about pushes them far away (b1 -67). The paper's rule is not stated. A population with x of SD 1 gives -8.1.

cause.summary: In Table 1 the discrete intercept's printed estimate and t (-0.898, -1369.34) imply an SE of 0.000656, printed as 0.00065 (cut, not rounded). The other three SEs and P(x>2.5) come back.

items.label: The paper against itself: Fig. 2's headings and Table 1's curve 2.011 + 23.9/n

cause.summary: Fig. 2's headings are means at six sizes; Table 1's curve 2.011 + 23.9/n gives the means it implies. Five of six headings lie 0.02 to 0.04 below the curve (2.003 at n = 1000 against 2.035), and Fig. 3's medians sit higher still (about 2.07 at n = 1000). Figs 2 and 3 cannot come from the run behind Table 1 and Fig. 1.

items.label: Abstract and Results: estimates biased away from zero, odds ratios away from one
Results: the fit is better for the continuous than for the discrete variable
Results and Fig. 2: the sampling distribution is skewed at small n and grows symmetric
Results and Fig. 3: extreme estimates become rarer as n grows
Methods: kernel regression derivatives confirm the convergence rate

cause.summary: The continuous coefficient's kernel derivative has the sign of -b1/n² everywhere and falls as n to the power -2.07. The discrete check fails because our discrete means have almost no 1/n trend (b1 -1.9, R² 0.03, see table1.discrete), which depends on the unstated handling of separated samples.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The discrete trend depends on the rule for separated samples
hypotheses.test: Discrete b1 under the three rules (tables.json): -1.9 (ours), -67 (only R's warnings), -128 (every fit)

items.label: Discussion: maximum likelihood is risky under n = 100 and adequate above 500 (Long 1997)

cause.summary: A citation of Long (1997), not a result of the paper.

Drawn on the published axes, 162 of our 281 means fall below them: our population sits lower (intercept 1.966 against 2.011) and our means scatter more. Moving our series by the difference of the intercepts raises the score from 12% to 54%; a population with x of SD 1 reaches 72%. Neither reaches the published points.

page.lede: We ran the study again: 281 sample sizes, 1,000 samples each, 281,000 logistic fits, and 20 more populations to see how far a rerun moves. Of {items} results, {exact} came back exactly and {agrees} agree; {partly} partly agree and {differs} differ.
page.items_caption: Each verdict is computed from the numbers by check_results.py. Ours is one population (seed 2724427).
page.claims_line: The main claim holds: in our run logistic regression pushes both coefficients away from zero, more at small n, and the sampling distribution is skewed at small n and grows symmetric. Table 1's slopes, SEs and R squared values and the figures' spreads do not come back; the causes are open (the paper's per-size means scatter less than any population of Additional file 1's design gives), and the intercepts move with the population draw.
came_back: Away from zero for both exposures, at every size.
Skewed at n = 100, near symmetric at n = 1000; fewer extreme estimates as n grows.
Additional file 1's R lines run unchanged, and P(x>2.5) = 0.2375.
buried: Table 1's slopes, SEs and R squared values: our means scatter more than the paper's.
The spreads of Figs 2 and 3: about 1.5 times wider in our run.
How the paper handled separated samples, and its seed.
page.matched_intro: Each line is a part of the paper and how close our run came.
matched: Intercepts within the spread of 20 populations; slopes and SEs not.
Most of our points fall off the published axes; no better than a wrong input.
Bias away from zero, skew and extremes all come back; the discrete kernel check does not.
page.closing: The bias came back. The paper's exact numbers did not.
page.front_note: The bias away from zero comes back; Table 1's slopes do not
